contenido: 1. The Pastors of the flock are aware that, in the fulfillment of their ministry as Bishops, they have a special divine grace. In the Roman Pontifical, during the solemn prayer of ordination, the principal ordaining Bishop, after invoking the outpouring of the Spirit who governs and guides, repeats the words of the ancient text of the Apostolic Tradition: "Holy Father, you who know the hearts, grant to this servant of yours, whom you chose for the episcopate, to be a good shepherd of your holy flock." In this way, the will of the Lord Jesus, the eternal Shepherd, who sent the Apostles as He was sent by the Father ( [+[0]+] ), and wanted His successors, that is, the Bishops, to be the shepherds of His Church until the end of the centuries, continues to be fulfilled.

2. We thank the Lord, then, for having granted us the grace to celebrate once again an Assembly of the Synod of Bishops and to have in it a profound experience of being Church. The X Ordinary General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops, which took place when the climate of the Great Jubilee of the year two thousand was still alive, at the beginning of the third Christian millennium, was reached after a long series of assemblies; some special ones, with the common perspective of evangelization in the different continents: Africa, America, Asia, Oceania and Europe; and other ordinary ones, the most recent, dedicated to reflecting on the great richness that the various vocations raised by the Spirit in the People of God represent for the Church. In this perspective, the attention paid to the proper ministry of the Bishops has completed the picture of that ecclesiology of communion and mission that must always be kept in mind.

3. In fact, each Bishop has the task of announcing hope to the world, starting from the preaching of the Gospel of Jesus Christ: hope "not only in what refers to penultimate realities but also, and above all, eschatological hope, which awaits the richness of the glory of God ( [+[0]+] ) which surpasses everything that has ever entered the heart of man ( [+[1]+] ) and is in no way comparable to the sufferings of the present tense ( [+[2]+] )». The perspective of theological hope, together with that of faith and charity, must completely shape the pastoral ministry of the Bishop.

4. Everyone will remember that the sessions of the Synod of Bishops took place during very dramatic days. In the Synod Fathers, the echo of the terrible events of September 11, 2001, which caused countless innocent victims and caused serious and unusual situations of uncertainty and fear to arise in the world for human civilization itself and the peaceful coexistence between nations, was still very much alive. New horizons of war and death were emerging that, adding to the already existing conflict situations, manifested in all their urgency the need to invoke the Prince of Peace so that the hearts of men would once again be available for reconciliation, solidarity and peace.

5. Thus, in delivering this Apostolic Exhortation, in which I take into consideration the body of reflection matured on the occasion of the X Ordinary General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops, from the first Lineamenta to the Instrumentum Laboris; from the interventions of the Synod Fathers in the Hall to the two Relations that have introduced and summarized them; from the enrichment of ideas and pastoral experience, manifested in the circuli minores, to the Propositions that were presented to me at the end of the synodal work so that I could offer the entire Church a document on the synodal theme: The Bishop, servant of the Gospel of Jesus Christ for the hope of the world, I address a fraternal greeting and send a kiss of peace to all the Bishops who are in communion with this Chair, first entrusted to Peter to be guarantor of unity and, as recognized by all, presides in love.

6. The Lord Jesus, during his earthly pilgrimage, announced the Gospel of the Kingdom and inaugurated it in himself, revealing its mystery to all men. He called men and women to follow Him and chose twelve among His disciples to “be with Him” ( [+[0]+] ). The Gospel according to Saint Luke specifies that Jesus made this choice after a night of prayer on the mountain ( [+[1]+] ). The Gospel according to Saint Mark, for its part, seems to qualify this action of Jesus as a sovereign decision, a constitutive act that grants identity to the chosen ones: "He instituted Twelve" ( [+[2]+] ). Thus the mystery of the election of the Twelve is revealed: it is an act of love, freely willed by Jesus in deep union with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

7. Considered in depth, the Christological dimension of pastoral ministry leads to understanding the Trinitarian foundation of the ministry itself. The life of Christ is Trinitarian. He is the eternal and only begotten Son of the Father and the one anointed by the Holy Spirit, sent into the world; He is the One who, together with the Father, sends the Spirit to the Church. This Trinitarian dimension, which is manifested in the entire way of being and acting of Christ, also shapes the being and acting of the Bishop. Rightly, then, the Synod Fathers wanted to explicitly illustrate the life and ministry of the Bishop in light of the Trinitarian ecclesiology of the doctrine of the Second Vatican Council.

8. "He instituted Twelve" ([+[0]+]). The dogmatic Constitution Lumen gentium introduces with this evangelical quote the doctrine on the collegial character of the group of the Twelve, constituted "as a College, that is, as a stable group, at the head of which it placed Peter, chosen from among themselves." In an analogous manner, when the Bishop of Rome succeeds Saint Peter and the other Bishops as a whole succeed the Apostles, the Roman Pontiff and the other Bishops are united with each other as a College.

9. The Gospel according to Saint Luke narrates that Jesus gave the Twelve the name of Apostles, which literally means sent, sent ( [+[0]+] ). In the Gospel according to Saint Mark we also read that Jesus instituted the Twelve "to send them to preach" ([+[1]+]). That means that the election and institution of the Twelve as Apostles is for mission. This first sending ( [+[2]+] ), reaches its fullness in the mission that Jesus entrusts to them, after the Resurrection, at the moment of the Ascension to Heaven. They are words that retain all their relevance: «Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always to the end of the world” ( [+[3]+] ). This apostolic mission was solemnly confirmed on the day of Pentecost with the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

10. The crowd followed Jesus when He decided to go up the mountain and call the Apostles to Himself. The disciples were many, but He chose only Twelve for the specific role of Apostles ( [+[0]+] ). In the Synodal Hall the saying of Saint Augustine was frequently heard: "I am a Bishop for you, I am a Christian with you."

11. With the same act of love with which he freely establishes them as Apostles, Jesus calls the Twelve to share his same life. This participation, which is a communion of feelings and desires with Him, is also a requirement inherent to participation in His same mission. The functions of the Bishop should not be reduced to a merely organizational task. Precisely to avoid this risk, both the preparatory documents of the Synod and numerous interventions in the Hall of the Synod Fathers insisted on what the reality of the episcopate as the fullness of the sacrament of Orders, in its theological, Christological and pneumatological foundations, entails for the personal life of the Bishop and the exercise of the ministry entrusted to him.

12. There is a biblical figure that seems particularly suitable to illustrate the profile of the Bishop as a friend of God, shepherd and guide of the people. It's about Moses. By focusing on him, the Bishop can find inspiration for his being and act as a shepherd, chosen and sent by the Lord, brave in leading his people towards the promised land, faithful interpreter of the word and law of the living God, mediator of the alliance, fervent and confident in prayer on behalf of his people. Like Moses, who after the conversation with God on the holy mountain returned to his people with a radiant face ( [+[0]+] ), the Bishop will also be able to bring to his brothers the signs of his being a father, brother and friend only if he has entered the dark and luminous cloud of the mystery of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Illuminated by the light of the Trinity, it will be a sign of the merciful goodness of the Father, a living image of the charity of the Son, a transparent man of the Spirit, consecrated and sent to lead the People of God along the paths of time on the pilgrimage towards eternity.

13. Only when he walks in the presence of the Lord can the Bishop truly consider himself a minister of communion and hope for God's holy people. In fact, it is not possible to be at the service of men without first being a "servant of God." And you cannot be a servant of God if you are not first a "man of God." That is why I said in the opening homily of the Synod: «The pastor must be a man of God; Their existence and their ministry are completely under divine lordship, and in the sublime mystery of God they find light and strength.

14. The maternal presence of the Virgin Mary, Mater spei et spes nostra, as invoked by the Church, must also be a support for the spiritual life of the Bishop. He must feel, therefore, an authentic and filial devotion to her, considering himself called to make Mary's fiat his own, to relive and update every day the dedication that Jesus made of Mary to the disciple, at the foot of the Cross, as well as that of the disciple who loved Mary ([+[0]+]). Likewise, it must be felt reflected in the unanimous and persevering prayer of the disciples and apostles of the Son, with his Mother, when they were waiting for Pentecost. In this icon of the nascent Church the indissoluble union between Mary and the successors of the apostles is expressed ( [+[1]+] ).

15. The Assembly of the Synod of Bishops indicated some necessary means to nourish and progress one's spiritual life. Among them is, first of all, the reading and meditation of the Word of God. Every Bishop must always entrust himself and feel entrusted "to God and to the Word of his grace, which has the power to build the building and give you the inheritance with all those who are sanctified" ([+[0]+]). Therefore, before being a transmitter of the Word, the Bishop, like his priests and the faithful, and even like the Church itself, has to be a listener of the Word. It must be "inside" the Word, to allow itself to be protected and nourished as in a mother's lap. With Saint Ignatius of Antioch, the Bishop also exclaims: "I have taken refuge in the Gospel, as if Christ himself were bodily present in it." Thus, he will always keep in mind that well-known exhortation of Saint Jerome, cited by the Second Vatican Council: "To ignore Scripture is to ignore Christ." In fact, there is no primacy of holiness without listening to the Word of God, which is the guide and nourishment of holiness.
16. Just as the paschal mystery is the center of the life and mission of the Good Shepherd, the Eucharist is also the center of the life and mission of the Bishop, like that of every priest.

17. A second means indicated by the Synod Fathers is prayer, especially that which is directed to the Lord with the recitation of the Liturgy of the Hours, which is always and specifically the prayer of the Christian community in the name of Christ and under the guidance of the Spirit.

18. The Lord proposes to all his disciples, but in a particular way to those who already during this life want to follow him more closely, like the Apostles, the path of evangelical counsels. These, in addition to being a gift of the Trinity to the Church, are a reflection of the Trinitarian life in the believer. They are especially so in the Bishop who, as successor of the Apostles, is called to follow Christ along the path of the perfection of charity. For this he is consecrated as Jesus is consecrated. His life is radical dependence on Him and total transparency before the Church and the world. In the life of the Bishop the life of Jesus must shine and, therefore, his obedience to the Father until death and death on the cross ([+[0]+]), his chaste and virginal love, his poverty which is absolute freedom from earthly goods.

19. Reflecting in himself these very human traits of Jesus, the Bishop also becomes a model and promoter of a spirituality of communion, oriented with careful attention to building the Church, so that everything, words and deeds, is carried out under the sign of filial submission in Christ and in the Spirit to the loving plan of the Father. As a teacher of holiness and minister of the sanctification of his people, the Bishop is called to faithfully carry out the will of the Father. The obedience of the Bishop must be lived having as a model – and it could not be otherwise – the very obedience of Christ, who said several times that he had come down from heaven not to do his will, but that of the One who had sent him ( [+[0]+] ).

20. The Synod Fathers, as a sign of collegial harmony, accepted the invitation that I made in the opening Liturgy of the Synod, so that the evangelical beatitude of poverty was considered one of the necessary conditions, in the current situation, to carry out a fruitful episcopal ministry. Also on this occasion, in the assembly of Bishops the figure of Christ the Lord was impressed, who "carried out the work of redemption in poverty and persecution" and invites the Church, with its pastors at the forefront, "to follow the same path to communicate to men the fruits of salvation."

21. "Receive this ring, a sign of fidelity, and remain faithful to the Church, Holy Bride of God." With these words of the Roman Pontifical of Ordination, the Bishop is invited to become aware that he assumes the commitment to reflect in himself the virginal love of Christ for all his faithful. He is called above all to foster reciprocal relationships among them inspired by the respect and esteem typical of a family where love flourishes in the sense of the apostle Peter's exhortation: “Love one another heartily and intensely. Behold, you have been born again, and not of a mortal father, but of an immortal one, through the living and lasting Word of God” ( [+[0]+] ).

22. In the Apostolic Letter Novo Millennio Ineunte I have stressed the need to "make the Church the home and school of communion." This observation has been widely echoed and has been taken up in the Synod Assembly. Obviously, the Bishop is the first who, in his spiritual path, has the task of being a promoter and animator of a spirituality of communion, striving tirelessly to make this one of the basic educational principles in all the areas in which man and Christian are modeled: in the parish, Catholic associations, ecclesial movements, Catholic schools or oratories. In a particular way, the Bishop must ensure that the spirituality of communion is favored and developed where future priests are educated, that is, in seminaries, as well as in novitiates and religious houses, in Institutes and in theological Faculties.

23. Spiritual realism leads to the recognition that the Bishop must live his own vocation to holiness in the context of external and internal difficulties, his own and others' weaknesses, daily unforeseen events, and personal and institutional problems. This is a constant situation in the lives of pastors, to which Saint Gregory the Great bears witness when he painfully notes: "Since I have shouldered the responsibility, it is impossible for me to maintain the meditation that I would like, being in need as I am for so many matters. I am, in fact, obliged to settle the causes, now of the various Churches, now of the monasteries, and to frequently judge the life and actions of particular individuals [...]. With my spirit scattered and torn with so many different concerns, how will I be able to refocus myself to dedicate myself entirely to preaching and the ministry of the word? [...] What am I, therefore, or what kind of watchman am I, that I am not situated, by my works, on the top of the mountain?».

24. In close relation to the Bishop's duty to tirelessly follow the path of holiness by living a Christ-centered and ecclesial spirituality, the synodal Assembly also raised the question of his ongoing formation. This, necessary for all the faithful, as emphasized in previous Synods and recalled in the successive Apostolic Exhortations Christifideles laici, Pastores dabo vobis and Vita consecrata, must be considered necessary especially for the Bishop, who has the responsibility for the common and concordant progress of the Church.

25. The Bishops always find encouragement in the example of holy Pastors, both for their life and their ministry and for their own spirituality and their effort to adapt apostolic action. In the homily of the closing Eucharistic Celebration of the Synod, I myself proposed the figure of holy Shepherds, canonized during the last century, as testimony of a grace of the Spirit that has never been lacking and will never be lacking in the Church.

26. The resurrected Jesus entrusted his apostles with the mission of "making disciples" of all people, teaching them to keep everything that he himself had commanded. Thus, the Church, the community of the disciples of the crucified and risen Lord, has been solemnly entrusted with the task of preaching the Gospel to all creatures. It is a task that will last until the end of time. From that first moment, it is no longer possible to think of the Church without this evangelizing mission. It is a conviction that the apostle Paul expressed in the well-known words: “Preaching the Gospel is no reason for my glory; It is rather a duty that falls on me. And woe to me if I did not preach the Gospel! ( [+[0]+] ).

27. The theme of the proclamation of the Gospel predominated in the interventions of the Synod Fathers, who repeatedly and in various ways affirmed how the living center of the proclamation of the Gospel is Christ crucified and risen for the salvation of all men.

28. The Second Vatican Council, following the line indicated by the tradition of the Church, affirms that the teaching mission of the Bishops consists of holily preserving and boldly announcing the faith.

29. With episcopal ordination each Bishop has received the fundamental mission of authoritatively announcing the Word. The Bishop, by virtue of the sacred Ordination, is an authentic teacher who preaches to the people entrusted to him the faith that must be believed and applied to the moral life. This means that the Bishops are vested with the same authority of Christ and that, for this fundamental reason, "when they teach in communion with the Roman Pontiff, they deserve the respect of all, since they are the witnesses of divine and Catholic truth." The faithful, for their part, must adhere to the decision that their Bishop has taken on matters of faith and customs in the name of Christ and accept it in a spirit of religious obedience. In this service to the Truth, the Bishop places himself before the community and is for it, to which he directs his pastoral care and for which he insistently raises his prayers to God.

30. The evangelization of culture and the inculturation of the Gospel are part of the new evangelization and, therefore, are a specific task of the episcopal function. In this regard, taking some of my previous expressions, the Synod repeated: "A faith that does not become culture is a faith not accepted, not fully thought out, not faithfully lived."

31. The ministry of the Bishop, as a preacher of the Gospel and custodian of faith in the People of God, would not be fully described if it were lacking a reference to the duty of personal coherence: his teaching must continue with the testimony and example of an authentic life of faith. If the Bishop, who teaches the community the Word heard with an authority exercised in the name of Jesus Christ, does not live what he teaches, he transmits a contradictory message to the community itself.

32. When discussing one of the first and fundamental functions of the Bishop, the ministry of sanctification, I think of the words that the apostle Paul addressed to the faithful of Corinth, as if placing before their eyes the mystery of their vocation: "Sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all who everywhere call on the name of Jesus Christ, our Lord" ([+[0]+]). The sanctification of the Christian is carried out in the baptismal bath, is corroborated in the sacrament of Confirmation and Reconciliation, and is nourished by the Eucharist, the most precious good of the Church, the sacrament that constantly builds it up as the People of God, the body of Christ and the temple of the Holy Spirit.

33. The Bishop exercises the ministry of sanctification through the celebration of the Eucharist and the other Sacraments, the divine praise of the Liturgy of the Hours, the presidency of other sacred rites and also through the promotion of liturgical life and authentic popular piety. Among the celebrations presided over by the Bishop, those in which the peculiarity of the episcopal ministry as the fullness of the priesthood is especially highlighted. This is what happens in the administration of the sacrament of Confirmation, of Holy Orders, in the solemn celebration of the Eucharist in which the Bishop is surrounded by his presbytery and other ministers - as in the liturgy of the Chrism Mass - in the dedication of churches and altars, in the consecration of virgins, as well as in other rites important to the life of the Church. particular. He visibly presents himself in these celebrations as the father and shepherd of the faithful, the "High Priest" of his people ([+[0]+]), who prays and teaches how to pray, intercedes for his brothers and, together with the people, implores and gives thanks to God, highlighting the primacy of God and his glory.

34. Although the Bishop exercises his ministry of sanctification throughout the diocese, it has its center in the cathedral church, which is like the mother church and the point of convergence of the particular Church.

35. In the current circumstances, the Synod Fathers wanted to draw attention to the importance of the ministry of sanctification exercised in the Liturgy, which must be celebrated in such a way as to make its didactic and educational force effective. This requires that liturgical celebrations be truly epiphany of the mystery. They must clearly express, therefore, the nature of divine worship, reflecting the genuine meaning of the Church that prays and celebrates the divine mysteries. Furthermore, if everyone participates appropriately in the liturgy, according to the various ministries, it will shine with its dignity and beauty.

36. The life and ministry of the Bishop must be impregnated with the presence of the Lord and his mystery. Indeed, the promotion throughout the diocese of the conviction that the liturgy is the spiritual, catechetical and pastoral center depends largely on the example of the Bishop.

37. At the center of the munus sanctificandi of the Bishop is the Eucharist, which he himself offers or commissions to be offered, and in which his function as "bursar" or minister of grace of the supreme priesthood is especially manifested.

38. In the current circumstances of the Church and the world, both in the young Churches and in the Countries where Christianity has been established for centuries, the recovery, especially for adults, of the great tradition of the discipline of Christian initiation is providential. This has been a timely provision of the Second Vatican Council, which in this way wanted to offer a path of encounter with Christ and the Church to many men and women touched by the grace of the Spirit and eager to enter into communion with the mystery of salvation in Christ, died and risen for us.

39. In their interventions, the Synod Fathers paid special attention to penitential discipline, underlining its importance and the special care that the Bishops, as successors of the Apostles, must pay to the pastoral care and discipline of the sacrament of Penance. I am pleased to have heard from them what is a deep conviction of mine, that is, that great interest must be placed in the pastoral care of this sacrament of the Church, a source of reconciliation, peace and joy for all of us, in need of the Lord's mercy and the healing of the wounds of sin.

40. The Synod Fathers confirmed the importance of popular piety in the transmission and development of the faith. In fact, as my predecessor Paul VI said, this piety entails great values, both with respect to God and to our brothers, thus becoming a true treasure of spirituality in the life of Christian communities.

41. The holiness of the people of God, to which the Bishop's ministry of sanctification is ordered, is a gift of divine grace and a manifestation of the primacy of God in the life of the Church. For this reason, in his ministry he must tirelessly promote an authentic pastoral and pedagogy of holiness, in order to carry out the program proposed in the fifth chapter of the Constitution Lumen Gentium on the universal vocation to holiness.

42. The Second Vatican Council, when dealing with the duty of governing the family of God and of habitually and daily care for the flock of the Lord Jesus, explains that the Bishops, in the exercise of their ministry as fathers and shepherds of their faithful, must behave as "those who serve", always inspired by the example of the Good Shepherd, who came not to be served but to serve and give his life for the sheep ( [+[0]+] ).

43. The Bishop is sent as a shepherd, in the name of Christ, to care for a portion of the People of God. Through the Gospel and the Eucharist he must make it grow as a reality of communion in the Holy Spirit. From this it follows that the Bishop represents and governs the Church entrusted to him, with the necessary power to exercise the pastoral ministry sacramentally received ([+[0]+]), which is participation in the same consecration and mission of Christ. For this reason, the Bishops "as vicars and legatees of Christ govern the particular Churches that have been entrusted to them, not only with their projects, with their advice and with their examples, but also with their authority and sacred power, which they exercise, however, only to build their flock in truth and holiness, remembering that the elder must become like the younger and the superior like the servant ( [+[1]+] )."

44. The ecclesial communion lived will lead the Bishop to a pastoral style that is increasingly open to the collaboration of all. There is a certain interrelation between what the Bishop must decide under his personal responsibility for the good of the Church entrusted to his care and the contribution that the faithful can offer him through advisory bodies, such as the diocesan synod, the presbyteral council, the episcopal council and the pastoral council.

45. Many interventions by the Synod Fathers referred to various aspects and moments in the life of the diocese. Thus, due attention was paid to the diocesan Curia as a structure from which the Bishop uses to express his own pastoral charity in its various aspects. The convenience of the economic administration of the diocese being entrusted to people who, in addition to being honest, are competent, was once again emphasized, so as to be an example of transparency for other similar ecclesiastical institutions. If a spirituality of communion is lived in the diocese, privileged attention will be paid to the poorest parishes and communities, also doing everything possible to allocate part of the economic resources to the most indigent Churches, especially in mission and migration lands.

46. Precisely in this perspective the importance of the pastoral visit stands out, an authentic time of grace and a special moment, even unique, for the meeting and dialogue of the Bishop with the faithful. Bishop Bartolomeu dos Mártires, whom I myself beatified a few days after concluding the Synod, in his classic work Stimulus Pastorum, also highly esteemed by Saint Charles Borromeo, defines the pastoral visit quasi anima episcopalis regiminis and describes it eloquently as an expansion of the spiritual presence of the Bishop among his faithful.

47. When describing the particular Church, the conciliar decree Christus Dominus rightly defines it as a community of faithful entrusted to the pastoral care of the Bishop "cum cooperatione presbyterii." In fact, between the Bishop and the priests there is a communio sacramentalis by virtue of the ministerial or hierarchical priesthood, which is participation in the one priesthood of Christ and, therefore, although to a different degree, by virtue of the one ordained ecclesial ministry and the one apostolic mission.

48. When delving deeper into the topic of the ministry of priests, the Synod Fathers focused their attention on the formation of candidates for the priesthood, which takes place in the Seminary. This formation, with all that it entails of prayer, dedication and effort, is a concern of capital importance for the Bishop. The Synod Fathers, in this regard, knowing well that the Seminary is one of the most precious assets for the diocese, dealt with it in detail, reaffirming the indisputable need for the Major Seminary, without neglecting the relevance that the Minor Seminary also has for the transmission of Christian values ​​with a view to following Christ.

49. As dispensers of sacred Orders, the Bishops also have a direct responsibility towards the permanent Deacons, who the Synodal Assembly recognizes as authentic gifts from God to announce the Gospel, instruct Christian communities and promote the service of charity in the family of God.

50. The post-synodal Apostolic Exhortation Vita consecrata already underlined the importance of consecrated life in the ministry of the Bishop. Relying on that text, the Fathers recalled in this last Synod that, in the Church as a communion, the Bishop must esteem and promote the specific vocation and mission of consecrated life, which belongs stably and firmly to the life and holiness of the Church.

51. In the lay faithful, who are the majority of the People of God, the missionary force of Baptism must stand out. To do this they need the support, encouragement and help of their Bishops, who lead them to develop the apostolate according to their own secular nature, based on the grace of the sacraments of Baptism and Confirmation. For this reason, it is necessary to promote specific training programs that enable them to assume responsibilities in the Church within the structures of diocesan and parish participation, as well as in the various services of liturgical animation, catechesis, teaching of the Catholic religion in schools, etc.

52. The Synod Fathers spoke many times in favor of the family, rightly called "domestic church", a space open to the presence of the Lord Jesus, sanctuary of life. Founded in the sacrament of Marriage, it is a community of primary importance, since in it both spouses and their children live their own vocation and are perfected in charity. The Christian family – it was emphasized in the Synod – is an apostolic community, open to the mission.

53. The Bishop, pastor and father of the Christian community, must pay particular attention to the evangelization and spiritual accompaniment of young people. A ministry of hope cannot fail to build the future together with those to whom the future is entrusted, that is, the young. Like "sentinels of the morning," they await the dawn of a new world. The experience of the World Youth Days, which the Bishops enthusiastically support, teaches us how many young people are willing to commit themselves to the Church and the world if they are offered authentic responsibility and are offered comprehensive Christian formation.

54. It is necessary to promote a vocational culture in its broadest sense, that is, young people must be educated to discover life itself as a vocation. Therefore, it is appropriate that the Bishop urge families, parish communities and educational institutes to help young people discover God's plan for their lives, accepting the call to holiness that God addresses to each one in an original way.

55. Writing to the Christians of Corinth, the apostle Paul remembers how much he suffered for the Gospel: «Frequent travels; river dangers; dangers of robbers; dangers of my race; dangers of the Gentiles; dangers in the city; dangers in unpopulated areas; dangers at sea; dangers between false brothers; work and fatigue; sleepless nights, many times; hunger and thirst; many days without eating; cold and nakedness. And apart from other things, my daily responsibility: concern for all the Churches” ( [+[0]+] ). From this he draws a passionate conclusion: «Who faints without me fainting? Who suffers scandal without me burning? ( [+[1]+] ). This same question challenges the conscience of each Bishop as a member of the Episcopal College.

56. The Second Vatican Council teaches that "the Bishops, as successors of the Apostles, have in themselves, in the dioceses entrusted to them, all the ordinary, proper and immediate power required for the exercise of their pastoral function without prejudice to the power that the Roman Pontiff has, by virtue of his function, to reserve some causes for himself or for another authority."

57. The ad limina Apostolorum visits are both a manifestation and a means of communion between the Bishops and the Chair of Peter. In fact, they consist of three main moments, each with its own meaning. First of all, the pilgrimage to the tomb of the princes of the Apostles Peter and Paul, which indicates the reference to the one faith, to which both bore witness in Rome with their martyrdom.

58. According to already consolidated experience, each General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops, which in some way is an expression of the episcopate, shows in a peculiar way the spirit of communion that unites the Bishops with the Roman Pontiff and the Bishops with each other, giving the opportunity to express a profound ecclesial judgment, under the action of the Spirit, on the various problems that affect the life of the Church.

59. In addition to the universal scope, there are many and varied ways in which episcopal communion and, therefore, concern for all sister Churches can be expressed, and in fact is expressed. Likewise, the reciprocal relations between the Bishops go far beyond their institutional meetings. Being well aware of the collegial dimension of the ministry that has been conferred on them must encourage them to practice among themselves, especially within their own Episcopal Conference, their Province and ecclesiastical Region, the various forms of sacramental brotherhood, which range from reciprocal welcome and consideration to charitable attention and concrete collaboration.

60. In the same perspective of communion between Bishops and between Churches, the Synod Fathers paid very particular attention to the Eastern Catholic Churches, reconsidering the venerable and ancient riches of their traditions, which are a living treasure that coexists with analogous expressions of the Latin Church. From both, the Catholic unity of the holy People of God is better illuminated.

61. Among the institutions of the Eastern Catholic Churches, the patriarchal Churches stand out. They belong to those groups of Churches that, as the Second Vatican Council affirms, by divine Providence, have been organically constituted over time and enjoy both their own liturgical discipline and customs and a common theological and spiritual heritage, always preserving the unity of faith and the only divine constitution of the universal Church. Their particular dignity comes from the fact that, as wombs of faith, they have given rise to other Churches, which are like their daughters and, therefore, linked to them to this day by closer ties of charity in sacramental life and in the mutual respect of rights and duties.

62. A concrete way to promote communion between the Bishops and solidarity between the Churches is to give new vitality to the very ancient institution of the ecclesiastical Provinces, where the Archbishops are an instrument and sign of both the brotherhood between the Bishops of the Province and their communion with the Roman Pontiff. In fact, given the similarity of the problems that each Bishop must face, as well as the fact that a limited number facilitates a greater and more effective consensus, a common pastoral work can certainly be planned in the assemblies of the Bishops of the same Province and, above all, in the Provincial Councils.

63. This is in no way intended to diminish the importance and usefulness of the Conferences of Bishops, whose institutional configuration was already outlined in the last Council and further specified in the Code of Canon Law and in the recent Motu proprio Apostolos suos. In the Eastern Catholic Churches there are analogous Institutions, such as the Assemblies of the Hierarchs of various Churches sui iuris, provided for by the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches "so that, by communicating the lights of prudence and experience and exchanging opinions, a holy cooperation of forces is obtained for the common good of the Churches, through which unity of action is encouraged, common works are supported, and good is better promoted. of religion and ecclesiastical discipline is observed more effectively.

64. The prayer of the Lord Jesus for unity among all his disciples ( [+[0]+] ) is a pressing call to each Bishop for a specific apostolic duty. Such unity cannot be expected to be the result of our efforts; It is above all a gift of the Holy Trinity to the Church. However, this does not exempt Christians from making every effort, starting with prayer, to accelerate the path towards full unity. In response to the prayers and intentions of the Lord, and to his oblation on the Cross to reunite lost children ( [+[1]+] ), the Catholic Church feels irreversibly committed to ecumenical dialogue, on whose effectiveness its witness in the world depends. It is necessary, therefore, to persevere on the path of dialogue of truth and love.

65. The Bishops, as members of the Episcopal College, are not only consecrated for a diocese, but for the salvation of all men. The Synod Fathers once again recalled this doctrine expounded at the Second Vatican Council to emphasize that each Bishop must be aware of the missionary nature of his own pastoral ministry. All of his pastoral action, therefore, must be characterized by a missionary spirit, to arouse and preserve in the minds of the faithful the ardor for the spread of the Gospel. That is why it is the Bishop's task to raise, promote and direct missionary activities and initiatives in his own diocese, including from the economic aspect.

66. In Holy Scripture the Church is compared to a flock, "whose shepherd will be God Himself, as He Himself announced. Although it is human shepherds who govern the sheep, yet it is Christ himself who unceasingly guides and feeds them; He, the Good Shepherd and Head of the shepherds. Is it not Jesus himself who calls his disciples pusillus grex and exhorts them not to be afraid, but to cultivate hope? ( [+[0]+] ).

67. In this area of ​​missionary spirit, the Synod Fathers referred to the Bishop as a prophet of justice. Today more than yesterday, the war of the powerful against the weak has opened deep divisions between the rich and the poor. The poor are legion! Within an unjust economic system, with very strong structural dissonances, the situation of the marginalized worsens day by day. Today there is hunger in many parts of the earth, while in others there is opulence. The victims of these dramatic inequalities are above all the poor, the young, the refugees. In many places, women are also debased in their dignity as persons, victims of a hedonistic and materialistic culture.

68. As I have repeated in other circumstances, dialogue between religions must be at the service of peace between peoples. Indeed, religious traditions have the necessary resources to overcome ruptures and promote reciprocal friendship and respect between peoples. The Synod called for the Bishops to promote meetings with representatives of the people to reflect carefully on the discord and wars that tear the world, in order to find possible paths for a common commitment to justice, concord and peace.

69. In the Bishop's pastoral action, special attention must not be lacking to the demands of love and justice that derive from the social and economic conditions of the poorest, abandoned, and mistreated people, in whom the believer perceives particular images of Jesus. Their presence in ecclesiastical and civil communities tests the authenticity of our Christian faith.

70. The Synod Fathers also recalled the ethical aspects of the ecological question. Indeed, the deep meaning of the call to globalize solidarity also includes, and with urgency, the question of creation and the resources of the earth. The "groaning of creation" to which the Apostle alludes ( [+[0]+] ) seems to present itself today in an inverse perspective, since it is no longer an eschatological tension awaiting the revelation of the children of God ( [+[1]+] ), but rather a spasm of death that tends to trap man himself in order to destroy him.

71. Concern for man drives the Bishop to imitate Jesus, the authentic "good Samaritan", full of compassion and mercy, who cares for man without any discrimination. Health care occupies a relevant place among current challenges. Unfortunately, there are still many forms of illness in different parts of the world and, although human science progresses exponentially in the research of new solutions or aids to better deal with them, new situations always appear that undermine physical and mental health.

72. Population movements have today acquired unprecedented proportions and are presented as mass movements that affect a large number of people. Many of them have been evicted or flee their own country due to armed conflicts, precarious economic conditions, natural disasters or political, ethnic and social confrontations. Although the situations are diverse, all these migrations raise serious questions for our communities regarding pastoral problems, such as evangelization and interreligious dialogue.

73. Faced with such a humanly complex panorama for the proclamation of the Gospel, the episode of the multiplication of the loaves narrated in the Gospels comes to mind, almost spontaneously. The disciples explain to Jesus their perplexity at the crowd that, hungry for his word, has followed him into the desert, and they propose to him: "Resign, mobs... Dismiss the people" ([+[0]+]). Perhaps they are afraid and truly do not know how to satisfy such a large number of people.

74. The Bishop's commitment at the beginning of a new millennium is thus outlined. It is the same as always: announcing the Gospel of Christ, salvation for the world. But it is a commitment characterized by urgent developments, which demand the consistent dedication of all members of the People of God. The Bishop must be able to count on members of the diocesan presbytery and deacons, ministers of the blood of Christ and charity; with the consecrated sisters and brothers, called to be in the Church and in the world eloquent witnesses of the primacy of God in the Christian life and of the power of his love in the fragility of the human condition; finally, with the lay faithful, who are for the Pastors a particular source of support and a special reason for encouragement.
